query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing 30–50% of Ta with V in the HfMoTaTiZr refractory alloy will lower its density while preserving its high yield strength at both room and elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr refractory alloy having a density of roughly 10.21 g/cm³, with a room-temperature yield strength around 1600 MPa and an elevated-temperature (≈1000 °C) yield strength of ~855 MPa.
generation.intervention: Substitute 30–50% of the Ta content in HfMoTaTiZr with the lighter element V, adjusting elemental ratios to retain a homogeneous solid solution.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests conducted at room temperature and near 1000 °C under tensile and/or compressive loading conditions, similar to those used in previous high-temperature and room-temperature evaluations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and retention of a BCC solid-solution phase that benefits from lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening despite the compositional change.
generation.mechanism: By replacing heavier Ta with lighter V, the overall density of the alloy is reduced. V’s addition is expected to maintain the necessary lattice distortion and dislocation pinning effects that underpin high yield strength, preserving mechanical performance at both room and elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable decrease in density (targeting below ~10 g/cm³) with yield strengths that remain close to the baseline (≈1600 MPa at room temperature and ≥850 MPa at 1000 °C).
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with high density and robust strength at both room and elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: Evaluations limited to as-cast alloys under standard tensile/compressive testing conditions at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimal replacement fraction between 30% and 50% and potential impacts on ductility and fracture toughness are not fully characterized and may require further tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two alloy series where 30% and 50% of Ta in the baseline HfMoTaTiZr alloy is replaced by V. Ensure all alloys are produced using identical as-cast processing parameters. Conduct mechanical tests (tensile/compressive) at room temperature and at ≈1000 °C.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the V-substituted alloys fail to show at least a 5% reduction in density and/or suffer a yield strength reduction greater than 10% at either room temperature or 1000 °C compared to the baseline HfMoTaTiZr alloy, the hypothesis will be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs) are generally consisted of four or more principal elements in either equi-atomic or near equi-atomic composition, and tend to form simple solid solution structures, e.g., face-centered cubic (fcc), body-centered cubic (bcc) and or hexagonal close-packed (hcp), instead of complex phases or intermetallic compounds [,]. HEAs have recently received much attention owing to their unprecedented promising properties, such as outstanding strength, excellent fracture toughness, remarkable wear and corrosion resistance, etc. [,,,,]. This concept provides enormous capabilities for the development of novel alloys for application in extreme environments [,]. Recently, refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) consisted of refractory elements, such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, V, Ti, Zr, etc., have attracted increasing attention by virtue of their superior mechanical properties at room and elevated temperature [,,,]. Unfortunately, their high density (up to 10–14 g/cm3) and consequent low specific strength restrict their engineering application.

ABSTRACTOver 150 refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have been proposed in the last decade. Early alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW still show an unparalleled yield strength of approximately 400 MPa at 1600°C. However, RHEAs with even elevated high-temperature strength are necessary in aerospace vehicles and nuclear reactors to cope with advanced technology in the future. Here, solid-solution strengthening calculation and melting point prediction are combined to design single-phase RHEA for attaining ultrahigh strength at 1600°C. The results show that Hf0.5MoNbTaW and HfMoNbTaW alloys after fully homogeneous treatment at 2100°C for 2 h reveal a homogenous body-centered cubic phase. HfMoNbTaW alloy exhibits a yield strength of 571 MPa at 1600°C, much higher than that of MoNbTaVW (477 MPa). It is found that a plateau of strength occurs from 800°C to 1200°C, which is important for raising the strength level of RHEAs at high temperatures. This strengthening mechanism is explained with the change of deformation mode from screw to edge dislocations, which contributes an edge-dislocation-induced strength.
